clue.text: Shipmaster fine after eclipse cheers part of UK, Westward Ho!

indicators.note: after means the piece for fine is placed after everything else

parts.note: to cap something is to outdo or eclipse it
ta is British slang for thanks, like cheers

indicators.note: in an across clue, going westward means reading right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: NI is Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: A travel note: a ship's master gives thanks on reaching the Devon resort of Westward Ho!
explanation.walkthrough: Westward Ho! is a seaside village in Devon, which the surface leans on; split up, 'Westward' becomes a reversal signal and 'Ho' stands alone. In an across answer, westward reads right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Hook commands the pirate ship Jolly Roger in Peter Pan, so he is a fictional shipmaster.

clue.text: Bit mean

definitions.meaning: a noun: a piece snipped off, from a plant or a newspaper
an adjective: hurtful, as a remark can be

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like verbs or a phrase ('a bit mean'), but one is a noun and the other an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: a snipped-off piece of a plant or newspaper, and wounding in the way an unkind remark is.

clue.text: Introductions for this writer, up first to speak

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: the setter calls themself this writer, which gives me

indicators.note: first to means only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A writer volunteers to give the introductions and stands up to speak first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ME into EM in a down entry; 'first to' takes S from speak.
explanation.definitionFit: A proem is a preface or preamble to a book or speech, so proems are opening pieces of writing.

clue.text: Banter like silly kid

indicators.note: silly letters behave foolishly and will not stay in their given order

explanation.surface: Someone trades jokes like a daft child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like a comparison joining the halves, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang: a toddler is at ankle height, so a small kid is jokingly called this.

clue.text: Loud guide from the south causing a stink

indicators.note: in a down entry, starting from the south means reading from the bottom upward

parts.note: a fin steers a fish, a surfboard or a rocket

explanation.surface: A noisy tour guide from the south of the country makes a stink.
explanation.walkthrough: FFIN is written upward to fill the light.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: a niff is a bad smell.

clue.text: Utterly dominate game, Chelsea full backs ultimately making mistakes

parts.note: to own an opponent is slang for to beat them utterly
go is a game, the Asian board game, or a turn in one

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letters of each of the words that follow

parts.note: the three words whose last letters are taken

explanation.surface: A football report: Chelsea dominate the match, but their full backs keep making errors in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: In football, full backs are defenders and Chelsea is a London club. 'ultimately' takes ALS, the final letters of those three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Own goals are balls a player puts into their own net, and figuratively any self-inflicted blunders.

clue.text: Taxing financial gain

definitions.meaning: an adjective: exhausting, as a steep climb is
a noun: a big profit, as in 'make a ___'

explanation.walkthrough: Read together, 'taxing financial gain' sounds like a tax policy; split it after 'Taxing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally exhausting, and the idiom for a sudden large profit.

clue.text: Having gone into herd, animal doctor misses opening in horse's joint

parts.note: a flock is a herd of sheep or goats

explanation.surface: A vet goes into the herd and fails to spot a problem with a horse's leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' is not a gap in a joint but the first letter of VET.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain anatomy: the joint just above a horse's hoof, with its tuft of hair.

clue.text: Female set Down clue, originally camouflaged to describe Liberal hippy

parts.note: to lower something is to set it down

indicators.note: originally means only the first letter of clue is used

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

indicators.note: to describe here means to draw around, so the word for camouflaged surrounds the Liberal letter

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal in British politics

explanation.surface: The setter talks about writing a disguised clue for a Liberal-voting hippy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like part of the clue's grid reference, but 'set Down' is one phrase meaning lower. 'describe' is meant in its geometric sense, to trace a line round; 'originally' takes the C of clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Flower children were 1960s hippies who wore flowers as symbols of peace and love.

clue.text: Maybe loyal group of Rowling readers occasionally fear the end for Cormoran Strike

definitions.text: Maybe loyal group of Rowling readers

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of fear shows up

parts.note: odd letters F, A of fear

indicators.note: the end of Cormoran is its last letter

explanation.surface: J.K. Rowling's readers fear the fate of her detective Cormoran Strike.
explanation.walkthrough: Cormoran Strike is Rowling's detective (written as Robert Galbraith), so 'Strike' reads as a name; here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'Maybe': devoted readers of one author form an organised following.

clue.text: I put notices up for Spooner, yet quarrel

definitions.note: the definition is the person speaking about their job; the answer is the noun for that person

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version of the phrase swaps them

parts.note: yet = still; it gives up its ST sound and takes the B
quarrel = bicker; it hands over its B and collects the ST

explanation.surface: A man pins up notices yet still argues.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' is the person being defined, talking about their job.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a posted notice, and the person who pastes them on walls describes their work this way.

clue.text: Arresting European suspect, impound drug smoked here

indicators.note: arresting means catching and holding, so the scrambled letters hold the European letter inside
suspect, as an adjective meaning dubious, signals that the letters of impound are not to be trusted in their order

explanation.surface: Police seize a European suspect and impound the drug at a raid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' reads as a noun for the arrested person, but it signals an anagram of IMPOUND, which 'Arresting' wraps around E.
explanation.definitionFit: An opium den is a place where people gathered to smoke opium, the narcotic made from poppies.

clue.text: Gathering agents must infiltrate mostly unescorted?

explanation.surface: Spies must slip into a party where people have come without partners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' looks like a verb (collecting agents), but it is a noun: a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: an informal get-together of a club or group.

clue.text: One seen around bed and seat following one's husband

parts.note: f. = following, as in page references

explanation.surface: Someone sits by the bed next to their husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' suggests a bedroom, but it is the sea bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a fish that lives near the sea bed is one seen around it.

clue.text: Part of cooked breakfast, say, extremely generous

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its outermost letters

explanation.surface: A generous serving as part of a fry-up.
explanation.walkthrough: A cooked breakfast is the British fry-up of bacon, sausage, toast and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: fried or scrambled, they are one standard item on the plate.

clue.text: Ignores the wishes of stupid boss, idle git wasting time

indicators.note: stupid means senseless, so the letters that follow are put into a new order
wasting means losing, so the word git loses the letter for time

parts.note: the word that loses a letter

explanation.surface: An office grumble about a dim manager and a lazy employee who throws away the working day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasting' takes T out of GIT to leave GI; 'stupid' then mixes BOSS, IDLE and GI into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To disoblige someone is to act against their convenience or wishes, refusing a favour.

clue.text: Undone by pressure, a bowler playing poorly

indicators.note: something undone has been taken apart, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler cracks under pressure and bowls badly.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the bowler delivers the ball; here the word is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from golf: scoring worse than the standard means performing under your usual form.

clue.text: Here, secured by sailor on bow of clipper, is one of two anchors?

indicators.note: the bow is the front of a ship, so the first letter of clipper

explanation.surface: A sailor on a clipper ship secures one of its two anchors.
explanation.walkthrough: The anchors are not a ship's but a news programme's presenters, which the question mark signals.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on anchor, the presenter of a broadcast: sharing that role with one other person.

clue.text: Quiet pal so excited about rook in trees

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up out of their order

explanation.surface: A quiet friend gets excited about a rook nesting in the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: The rook is not the bird in the trees but R from chess.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: tall, fast-growing trees of the willow family.

clue.text: Case online tuition covers

indicators.note: the phrase covers, or contains, the answer inside it

explanation.surface: A legal case about online teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is a crossword favourite, from French, for a small ornamental holder.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific kind of case: a small decorative one for needles, pins or cosmetics.

clue.text: Firm to accommodate working after dark very soon?

explanation.surface: A firm takes on extra work in the evening to be ready soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as a company; it is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description, marked by '?': the coming evening is both after dark and not far off.

clue.text: Prior to game of chance, lid of Biro is under the table

indicators.note: the lid sits on top, so the first letter in a down entry

parts.note: lotto, a lottery or bingo-like game

explanation.surface: Before the lottery draw, the cap of a pen has fallen under the table.
explanation.walkthrough: A Biro is a ballpoint pen. 'Under the table' is the drunk's position, not the pen lid's.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone who has drunk so much they slide off their chair is very drunk.

clue.text: Ad-lib technique in rally cut short

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter of the word for rally is removed

parts.note: to rally, as a patient does, is to improve

explanation.surface: A speaker in a rally has their unscripted speech cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rally' looks like a noun for a political meeting, but it is the verb meaning to recover; 'cut short' then drops its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Improv is improvisation in performance, making up dialogue or comedy on the spot without a script.

clue.text: Author Deighton's visiting Omsk, busy Russian city

indicators.note: visiting means staying inside, so the author's name goes inside the jumbled letters
busy means bustling with activity, so the letters of Omsk are stirred up

parts.note: Len Deighton is the British spy novelist, and the possessive gives his name plus S

explanation.surface: The spy writer Len Deighton travels to the busy Siberian city of Omsk.
explanation.walkthrough: Omsk is itself a Russian city, which tempts it as the answer; 'busy' rearranges it to SMOK, and 'visiting' puts LENS (Deighton's) inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Smolensk is an ancient city in western Russia on the Dnieper, near the border with Belarus.

clue.text: Sudden shot

definitions.meaning: an adjective: done on the spur of the moment, as an election can be

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sudden shot' reads as a gunshot; split it into an adjective and a photo.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally, sudden or hurried, and a casual photograph.

clue.text: Poker Face, absolutely rubbish

parts.note: dead = absolutely, as in dead right
to pan is to rubbish, criticise harshly

explanation.surface: A reviewer calls the song Poker Face absolutely rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to the Lady Gaga song, but the definition is simply an expressionless face.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym phrase: a face that gives nothing away, as a card player's must.

clue.text: Figure Italian team will include Angelo in the middle

indicators.note: Angelo in the middle is just its central letters

explanation.surface: An Italian football team signs a player called Angelo to play in midfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' could be a shape or a person; here it is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain mathematical sense: a whole number is a figure.

clue.text: Ailment cheeky son lies about? That catches relative out for starters

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the cheeky son lies facing the other way
starters come first, so take the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A cheeky son fakes an illness to skip school, until a relative catches him out.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the first half, but the second half is still wordplay: 'That' is not a pointer back but letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sore throat caused by streptococcus bacteria is one ailment.
